clue.text: Spam gets overlooked, initially, in feasts

indicators.note: the opening letter is the one overlooked, so the word loses its start

blocks.note: spam is junk email
taken as written, before its first letter goes

explanation.surface: Unwanted emails pile up unread while someone is busy at banquets.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spam' looks like the tinned meat at a feast, but it is the email sense. GETS loses its G to give ETS.
explanation.definitionFit: Junkets are lavish outings or banquets, often enjoyed at someone else's expense, so feasts is a fair synonym.

clue.text: Steve, whose patience was tried by Windows, ultimately

definitions.note: a first name standing for the surname that goes with it

indicators.note: ultimately points to the very end, so only the final letter of the word is kept

blocks.note: the biblical Job, proverbial for his patience under trial
the last letter of Windows

explanation.surface: Apple's boss was famously exasperated by Microsoft's rival operating system, Windows.
explanation.walkthrough: Steve Jobs founded Apple, whose Mac competed with Microsoft Windows; 'Windows' here only supplies its last letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Steve Jobs was the co-founder of Apple, so the first name Steve points to his surname.

clue.text: Regularly enjoys the food

indicators.note: regularly means at even intervals, so every second letter of the following words is kept

blocks.note: the second, fourth, sixth and eighth letters

explanation.surface: Someone habitually relishes what is served.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the' does double duty: it lends its H to the letters taken, and also reads as the article before 'food'.
explanation.definitionFit: Nosh is informal British slang for food or a meal.

clue.text: I name Rex Duff as moderator

indicators.note: duff is British slang for useless or broken, so the letters before it are spoiled and rearranged

blocks.note: the fodder

explanation.surface: Someone appoints a man called Rex Duff to moderate, as if naming him at a ceremony.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rex Duff' reads as a full name, but Duff is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: In British exams a moderator is an examiner who checks that marking is consistent across schools.

clue.text: Quarter-pound cephalopod

blocks.note: south, one of the four quarters of the compass
quid is British slang for a pound sterling

explanation.surface: A cephalopod sold by weight, a quarter-pound piece at the fishmonger's.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Quarter-pound' reads as one weight, but splits into a compass point and slang for a pound coin.
explanation.definitionFit: A squid is a ten-armed sea mollusc of the class Cephalopoda, alongside octopus and cuttlefish.

clue.text: Sailor's drunk, with red cheeks

blocks.note: AB is an able seaman, an ordinary sailor; the 's joins it to what follows
a lush is a heavy drinker

explanation.surface: A seaman has had too much and his face is flushed.
explanation.definitionFit: Ablush is a literary adjective meaning blushing, so a person ablush has reddened cheeks.

clue.text: Supported motorists who were retired?

indicators.note: motorists who were retired are tucked up inside, so one word sits within the other

blocks.note: someone who has retired for the night has gone to bed
the RAC is the Royal Automobile Club, a British motoring organisation

explanation.surface: Someone gave backing to drivers who had stopped working.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Retired' suggests pensioners, but here it means gone to bed: the motoring club is placed inside the bed.
explanation.definitionFit: To brace something is to prop or reinforce it, so braced means supported or held firm.

clue.text: Smooth single containing ice and slice of lemon

indicators.note: containing means holding something within, so the next pieces go inside the first word
a slice is a small piece, here just the first letter of the word

blocks.note: single, as in not married
a rink is a sheet of ice for skating
the first letter of lemon

explanation.surface: A smooth single measure of spirit served with ice and a slice of lemon, like a gin.
explanation.walkthrough: The bar-order picture of a drink on the rocks misleads: 'ice' is a skating surface and 'single' means not married.
explanation.definitionFit: Something unwrinkled has no creases or folds, so it is smooth.

clue.text: Bandit king perhaps buried beneath road

indicators.note: in a down clue, something buried beneath another lies below it, so that piece is written second

blocks.note: a highway is a main road
a chess king is one of the men on the board; 'perhaps' marks it as an example

explanation.surface: An outlaw monarch lies buried under a road.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'buried beneath' puts the second piece under the first, so the road comes first.
explanation.definitionFit: A highwayman was a robber on horseback who held up travellers on the road, a kind of bandit.

clue.text: Coach saying you must ultimately make a strenuous effort

indicators.note: ultimately points to the final position, so only the last letter of that word counts

blocks.note: a coach is a long-distance bus
a tag is a stock saying or catchphrase
the letter U is said the same as you, as in text-speak
the last letter of must

explanation.surface: A sports coach tells the players that in the end they have to try their hardest.
explanation.walkthrough: The coach seems to be a trainer giving a pep talk, but is just a bus.
explanation.definitionFit: To bust a gut is an informal idiom for straining every effort to achieve something.

clue.text: Listen to bug or insect

blocks.note: first meaning: as a verb, to eavesdrop, listening in as a hidden bug does
second meaning: a small creature with pincers at its tail

explanation.surface: Instructions to hear out a creepy-crawly, or another insect.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bug' seems to be the creature, but belongs to the listening sense, as in bugging a room.
explanation.definitionFit: As a verb the word means to eavesdrop, and as a noun it names a common insect with tail pincers.

clue.text: Where a gang is holding US president

indicators.note: the words before it hold the answer inside them, spread across their letters

blocks.note: running across the word break of the first three words

explanation.surface: A question of where a gang is keeping an American president hostage.
explanation.definitionFit: Ronald Reagan was the 40th President of the United States, serving from 1981 to 1989.

clue.text: Summary inaccurately revised by international bridge partners

indicators.note: something put together inaccurately is not in the right order, so the letters must be rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written
I is the abbreviation for international
East and West are a partnership at the bridge table

explanation.surface: A précis carelessly edited by a pair of international bridge players.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Revised' looks like the anagram signal, but it is fodder; the signal is 'inaccurately'.
explanation.definitionFit: A bird's-eye view is a broad overview seen from above, hence a general summary of a subject.

clue.text: Administrative bully rang Amelia

indicators.note: to bully is to push around, so the letters after it are pushed into a new order

blocks.note: the fodder

explanation.surface: A bossy office type telephoned a woman called Amelia.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bully' reads as a noun for the caller, but it is a verb signalling the rearrangement.
explanation.definitionFit: Managerial means relating to management, the running and organising of an office or business.

clue.text: US financial interests large and small may, perhaps, get into Disney

indicators.note: to get into something is to enter it, so these pieces go inside the name that follows

blocks.note: Walt Disney, the animator; his first name holds the rest
L is the clothing-size abbreviation for large
S is the clothing-size abbreviation for small
may is hawthorn, a tree; 'perhaps' marks it as an example

explanation.surface: American money-makers big and little might try to buy into the Disney company.
explanation.walkthrough: 'may' looks like the verb, but is the hawthorn blossom, so it stands for a tree.
explanation.definitionFit: Wall Street, the New York finance district, is used as shorthand for American financial and banking interests.

clue.text: Asking anew about moments when realisation dawns

indicators.note: about suggests letters turned around and moved, so the words before it are rearranged

blocks.note: the fodder

explanation.surface: Someone poses questions again about the moments when things finally make sense.
explanation.walkthrough: 'anew' looks like the signal for rearranging, but it is part of the fodder; the signal is 'about'.
explanation.definitionFit: An awakening is a sudden realisation or coming to awareness of something.

clue.text: Surrounded by Dotty, Dora and Sally

indicators.note: dotty means crazy or scatty, so the letters of the name beside it are scrambled

blocks.note: being surrounded by something is being in it
the fodder

explanation.surface: Someone is hemmed in by three women, Dotty, Dora and Sally.
explanation.walkthrough: Dotty and Sally look like two more names, but one is the signal and the other the definition: a sally is a sudden sortie by troops.
explanation.definitionFit: A sally is a sudden attack out of a defended place, and an inroad is a hostile raid into territory.

clue.text: Important economist is half-cut

indicators.note: half-cut means cut in half, so only the first half of the name survives

blocks.note: John Maynard Keynes, the famous British economist

explanation.surface: A leading economist is a bit drunk.
explanation.walkthrough: Half-cut is British slang for tipsy, but here the six-letter name is literally cut in half.
explanation.definitionFit: Key as an adjective means crucial or of central importance.

clue.text: Reportedly shows disapproval over son having drinking sessions

indicators.note: reportedly means as heard said, so the word goes by its sound, not its spelling

blocks.note: boos, the noise a disapproving crowd makes, said the same as alcohol
finished, as in time is up
S is the abbreviation for son

explanation.surface: A parent tuts loudly at their son's habit of going out drinking.
explanation.definitionFit: Booze-ups are informal British for parties or outings with a lot of heavy drinking.

clue.text: Completely boring instrument is heard

indicators.note: is heard means the word is taken by its sound when spoken

blocks.note: an awl is a pointed tool for making holes

explanation.surface: A dull musical instrument can be heard throughout.
explanation.walkthrough: 'boring' suggests tedious music, but means drilling: the tool bores holes.
explanation.definitionFit: All used adverbially, as in all alone, means completely or entirely.

clue.text: Nana and silly pirate providing central characters in musical entertainment

indicators.note: the central characters are the middle letters, so only the core of the word is kept

blocks.note: both are pet names for a grandmother
silly used as a noun for a fool, as in 'you silly'
the two middle letters of pirate

explanation.surface: A grandmother and a daft pirate supply the leading roles in a stage show.
explanation.walkthrough: 'silly' looks like an adjective for the pirate, but is a noun on its own.
explanation.definitionFit: Grand opera is serious opera sung throughout, on a large scale, a form of musical entertainment.

clue.text: Is about to tackle a remote expedition

indicators.note: about means turned round, so the short word before it is read backwards
to tackle something is to get hold of it, so the outer word grips the rest

blocks.note: taken as written, then turned round
taken as written
far means distant

explanation.surface: Someone is about to take on a faraway trip.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Is about to' reads naturally as 'is going to', but 'about' turns the word round and 'to tackle' is a separate signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A safari is an overland expedition, especially in Africa, to watch or hunt animals.

clue.text: Spectacular lack of restraint as Anglicans leave South Africa

definitions.note: a noun here: a lavish show

indicators.note: when one group leaves, the other takes its place in the word

blocks.note: extravagance is excess, a lack of restraint
CE is the Church of England
ZA is the international code for South Africa

explanation.surface: An Anglican exodus from South Africa is a show of excess.
explanation.walkthrough: The CE at the end of EXTRAVAGANCE gives way to ZA.
explanation.definitionFit: An extravaganza is an elaborate, spectacular entertainment, and a spectacular as a noun is just such a show.

clue.text: Winning American poll

blocks.note: A is the abbreviation for American
poll is an old word for the head

explanation.surface: A US opinion survey shows who is in the lead.
explanation.walkthrough: 'poll' looks like an election survey, but is the archaic word for the head, as in poll tax.
explanation.definitionFit: Being ahead means being in front, as a team that is leading is winning.

clue.text: Fellow has got one's number

blocks.note: F is the abbreviation for fellow
from the speaker's view, 'one has got' becomes I've got, contracted

explanation.surface: A man has worked someone out and got their number.
explanation.definitionFit: Five is a whole number, one more than four, so it is a number.

clue.text: Newspaper boss supports you and me being exploited

indicators.note: in a down clue, a piece that supports another holds it up from below, so it comes second

blocks.note: you and me together are us
ED is short for editor

explanation.surface: An editor backs us while we are being taken advantage of.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'supports' means sits under, so the editor goes beneath the other piece.
explanation.definitionFit: To be used is to be taken advantage of, which is exploited in the unkind sense.

clue.text: Place one finds cold to walk around

indicators.note: around means turned back on itself, so the verb before it is read backwards

blocks.note: the Roman numeral for one
C is the abbreviation for cold, as on a tap
to pace is to walk steadily

explanation.surface: A frozen spot where you might find it cold to go for a stroll.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface invites reading 'Place one finds cold' as the whole definition; only 'Place' defines.
explanation.definitionFit: An icecap is a region permanently covered in ice, such as at the poles, so it is a place.

clue.text: Impressive SUV I used to get round volcano

indicators.note: the earlier words get round the answer, wrapping it inside their run of letters

blocks.note: running through the end of the first word and the following three

explanation.surface: A big four-by-four was driven around a mountain.
explanation.walkthrough: An SUV is a sports utility vehicle; the volcano near Naples lies within the run of letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Vesuvius is the active volcano above the Bay of Naples that buried Pompeii in AD 79.

clue.text: The French excursion makes us cast off restraints!

blocks.note: le is French for the
a trip is an outing

explanation.surface: A holiday in France lets everyone go wild.
explanation.definitionFit: To let rip is an idiom for acting without restraint, letting go fully.

clue.text: Little girl heading off from Belgian port in balloon

indicators.note: heading off means losing the head, so the first letter of the port is dropped

blocks.note: Di is a short form of a girl's name such as Diana
Ostend is a port on the Belgian coast

explanation.surface: A young girl sets off from Ostend in a hot-air balloon.
explanation.walkthrough: 'balloon' reads as the craft, but it is a verb: to swell up.
explanation.definitionFit: To distend is to swell outwards from internal pressure, as a balloon does when inflated.
